title: As a developer, I can add memories from conversations and retrieve them later with semantic search, so context persists across sessions
As a developer, I can rely on the memory layer to update, supersede, or merge memories when new information contradicts what was stored
As an ml-engineer, I can see published memory-quality benchmark results (e.g. LongMemEval, LoCoMo) backing the product's recall-accuracy claims
As a developer, I can steer retrieval with metadata filters, keyword/hybrid search modes, or reranking instead of accepting a single fixed similarity search
As an ml-engineer, I can store memories as a knowledge graph of entities and relationships so multi-hop and entity-centric questions are answerable
As an ml-engineer, I can track when facts became valid or invalid (temporal reasoning) so the memory distinguishes current from outdated information
As an ml-engineer, I can customize the memory schema — entity types, edge types, or ontology — to match my domain
As a developer, I can get summaries of past sessions or threads so an agent can pick up where the last conversation left off
As a developer, I can retrieve a token-budgeted, prompt-ready context block assembled from relevant memories in one call
As a developer, I can ingest documents, JSON, and business data into memory — not just chat transcripts
As a developer, I can store images, PDFs, or other files as memory inputs and recall information from them later
As a platform-engineer, I can see documented retrieval-latency targets or measured numbers (e.g. p50/p95) backing the product's speed claims
As a platform-engineer, I can ingest at scale with async or batch processing and check the status of background memory operations
As a developer, I can scope memories per user, agent, or application so one tenant's memories never leak into another's retrieval
As a platform-engineer, I can govern who and what can read or write memory with roles, policies, or access-control lists, and audit that access
As a developer, I can share selected memory across multiple agents or users (team or group memory) while keeping private memory private
As a developer, I can make memories expire or decay — via TTL, expiration dates, or recency weighting — so stale facts stop surfacing
As a platform-engineer, I can delete a user's memories on demand — single memory, per-entity, or full erasure — to satisfy privacy requirements
As a platform-engineer, I can export memories in a machine-readable format so the memory store is portable and not a lock-in trap
As a platform-engineer, I can self-host the memory layer from open-source code (e.g. via Docker) on infrastructure I control
As a developer, I can run the memory layer fully locally — embedded in-process or against local models — without any cloud dependency
As a developer, I can build against official SDKs in at least Python and TypeScript with equivalent memory APIs
As a developer, I can drop the memory layer into agent frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or the Vercel AI SDK via documented first-party integrations
As a developer, I can wire memory into real-time voice pipelines (e.g. LiveKit, Pipecat, ElevenLabs) with documented integrations fast enough for live conversation
As a platform-engineer, I can see published pricing with a free tier and per-unit rates so I can project memory costs before committing
As an AI-native user, my agent can manage its own memory mid-conversation — adding, searching, updating, and deleting memories through tools or API calls it invokes itself
As an AI-native user, I can connect off-the-shelf assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) to the same memory so every tool I use shares what it knows about me
As an AI-native user, the memory layer decides for itself what is worth remembering — extracting salient facts from raw conversation and consolidating them in the background
